title: MCP 2026 Protocol Revision: Going Stateless
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is undergoing its largest revision since launch. A release candidate for the `2026-07-28` specification was published in mid-July 2026, with the final spec shipping on July 28, 2026. The headline change: MCP's transport layer moves from a stateful, session-based model to a **stateless core** that runs on ordinary HTTP infrastructure.

This page covers what changed and why it matters for anyone running or building MCP servers.

---

## Why Stateless Matters

Prior MCP versions required an `initialize` handshake that established a protocol-level session between client and server. In practice this meant:

- Load balancers needed **sticky sessions** to route every request from a given client back to the same server instance
- Horizontally scaling an MCP server meant sharing session state across instances (e.g., via a shared cache), adding operational complexity
- A server restart or instance swap could silently break an in-flight session

The 2026-07-28 revision removes the initialize handshake and the protocol-level session entirely. Servers can now scale behind a **plain round-robin load balancer** with no sticky-session requirement and no shared session store.

---

## New Streamable HTTP Headers

To let infrastructure route intelligently without inspecting request bodies, the Streamable HTTP transport now requires two headers on every call:

- **`Mcp-Method`** — the MCP operation being invoked (e.g., `tools/call`, `resources/read`)
- **`Mcp-Name`** — the specific tool or resource name being targeted

This lets a load balancer or API gateway route, rate-limit, or shard traffic by operation type without parsing JSON-RPC payloads.

---

## Caching Hints: `ttlMs` and `cacheScope`

`tools/list` and `resources/read` responses can now carry two new fields:

- **`ttlMs`** — how long (in milliseconds) the response should be considered fresh
- **`cacheScope`** — whether the response is safe to cache and share across users (e.g., `"public"`) or must stay scoped to a single caller (e.g., `"private"`)

This gives clients explicit permission to cache tool listings and resource reads instead of re-fetching on every call, which matters a lot for high-traffic MCP clients like published Artifacts with live connector data.

---

## New Extensions: MCP Apps and Tasks

Two extensions ship alongside the core revision:

- **MCP Apps** — lets a server return a server-rendered UI (not just JSON/text) that a compatible client can display inline, enabling richer tool results than plain text or markdown.
- **Tasks** — a standard way to represent long-running work that outlives a single request/response cycle, so a client can kick off a job, disconnect, and poll or subscribe for status later instead of holding a connection open.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)

The Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension was promoted to **stable** status in this revision. It gives organizations a centralized way to control which users and agents can access which MCP servers by routing authorization decisions through the org's existing identity provider (SSO/OIDC), rather than each server managing its own auth. Adopters at launch include Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta.

---

## Ecosystem Adoption

- **X (formerly Twitter)** launched a hosted MCP server exposing its platform API to MCP-compatible clients.
- **Microsoft** is building a catalog of 60+ ready-made MCP servers for enterprise systems, reachable from Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, and Azure AI Foundry.
- Claude Code and Claude.ai Artifacts both consume the new caching hints to support live, connector-backed dashboards published as artifacts.

---

## Practical Impact for MCP Server Authors

- Existing stateful servers should plan a migration off the `initialize` handshake before older-protocol clients are deprecated.
- Add `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` headers to Streamable HTTP responses to remain compatible with routing infrastructure built against the new spec.
- Set accurate `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` values on `tools/list` and `resources/read` responses — omitting them forces clients to treat every response as uncacheable and private by default.
- Organizations with many internal MCP servers should evaluate Enterprise-Managed Authorization instead of building bespoke per-server auth.
